hook.support: You scroll past hundreds of videos a day. You remember maybe one. Why that one? It grabbed you fast and had **one** clear message.
hook.core: Every day you scroll past hundreds of videos. You remember maybe one. It wasn't the most expensive, or the loudest. It made you **feel** something in the first three seconds, and it had **one** thing to say. You can make one of those.

why.support: Good videos are planned. Choose your **purpose**, your **audience** and **one message**. Write a **script**. Plan your shots. Then film it.
why.core: Making content that counts is a writing job. Before anyone presses record, someone decides the **purpose**, the **audience** and the **one message**. They write a **script**, plan every **shot** in a **storyboard**, and choose the sound. Those choices are what make people stop, watch, and remember.
why.extend: Effective multimodal content is designed: purpose, audience and message come first, then language, image, sound and sequence are selected to serve them. Planning through scripts and storyboards turns an idea into a text that positions its audience deliberately.

articles.title: How to make content that counts

body.support:
Good content is **planned**.

**1. Plan.** What's it for? Who's it for? What's your **one message**?

**2. Hook them fast.** Start with a question or a surprise.

**3. Write a script.** Short sentences. Words you'd really say. Read it **out loud**.

**4. Storyboard it.** Draw each **shot**. Write what we see and hear.

- **Close-up**: feels personal.
- **Wide shot**: shows the place.
- Big, bright things get noticed first.

**5. Sound.** Music sets the mood. Add **captions**.

**6. Call to action.** Tell people what to do.

**7. Check it.** Are your facts true? Did everyone say yes to being filmed?

**8. Share safely.** Under 16? Share it in class or on the school website.
body.core:
Most content gets scrolled past in a second. Content that counts is **planned**. Here's how.

**1. Purpose, audience, one message.** Why are you making it: to inform, persuade, or entertain? Who's it for? What's the **one** thing you want them to remember? If you can't say your message in one sentence, it's not ready.

**2. Hook them fast.** The first three seconds decide whether people keep watching. Start with a question (*Ever sent something you wish you could unsend?*), a surprise, or a close-up.

**3. Write a script.** Even a 30-second video needs one. Use short sentences and words you'd actually say. Read it **out loud**: if you trip over it, rewrite it. Plan your **voice** too: where you'll pause, which word you'll stress, how fast you'll talk.

**4. Storyboard it.** Plan each **shot** in a box: what we **see** and what we **hear**.

- **Close-ups** feel personal. **Wide shots** show where we are.
- Whatever is **biggest, brightest or in the middle** gets noticed first. That's called **salience**.
- The **order** of shots tells the story: problem, then solution.

**5. Choose the sound.** Music sets the mood. A sudden silence makes people pay attention. Add **captions**, because some people watch with the sound off, and some can't hear it.

**6. End with a call to action.** Tell people what to do: *Pause before you post.*

**7. Check before you share.**

- Are your facts true? Can you name your source?
- Did everyone in it say yes to being filmed and shared?
- Do you have the right to use that music?

**8. Share it safely.** Since December 2025, under-16s can't have accounts on platforms like TikTok, Instagram and YouTube. So share it in class, at assembly, or on your school's website or newsletter, with permission. If you're 16 or over, remember it becomes part of your digital footprint.
body.extend:
Content that cuts through is designed, not improvised.

**1. Define purpose, audience and message.** Decide whether you aim to inform, persuade or entertain; who the audience is; and the single message they should retain. If it won't fit in one sentence, refine it.

**2. Engineer the hook.** The opening seconds determine retention. Questions, surprises and close-ups create immediate engagement.

**3. Script for the ear.** Spoken scripts need short sentences and natural vocabulary. Rehearse aloud and mark **voice** choices: pauses, emphasis and pace.

**4. Storyboard deliberately.** Plan each **shot** (what's seen and heard).

- **Framing:** close-ups create intimacy; wide shots establish context.
- **Salience:** size, brightness, colour and central placement direct attention.
- **Sequence:** the order of shots builds meaning, typically problem then resolution.

**5. Design the sound.** Music establishes mood, silence creates emphasis, and **captions** make the text accessible to people watching without sound or who are Deaf or hard of hearing.

**6. Close with a call to action.**

**7. Verify before publishing.** Check facts against sources, get consent from everyone who appears, and use only music you have the rights to.

**8. Publish responsibly.** Since December 2025, under-16s can't hold accounts on platforms such as TikTok, Instagram and YouTube. Use school channels, class screenings or assemblies, with permission. For 16 and over, published content becomes part of your digital footprint.

caseStudies.title: Meet Graham

body.support:
The **TAC** wanted people to know one thing: our bodies can't survive car crashes.

In **2016**, it tried something new. Experts worked out how a body would need to change to survive a crash. An artist, **Patricia Piccinini**, made a sculpture of that body. He's called **Graham**.

Graham looks strange. He has **no neck**, so he can't break it.

People went to see him at the **State Library of Victoria**. There was an app and school lessons too.

Why did it work? **One message**. And you could **see** it.
body.core:
The **TAC** (Transport Accident Commission) wanted Victorians to understand one thing: our bodies aren't built to survive car crashes, even slow ones.

Facts and numbers hadn't been enough. So in **2016**, the TAC tried something different.

It asked two experts, a **trauma surgeon** and a **crash investigator** from Monash University, how a human body would need to change to survive a crash. Then a Melbourne artist, **Patricia Piccinini**, made a life-like sculpture of that body. They called him **Graham**.

Graham looks strange. He has **no neck**, so he can't break it. Every part of him was designed around how real crashes injure people.

Graham was shown at the **State Library of Victoria**, then toured Victoria. People could use an app to look **under his skin**, and schools got lessons to go with him.

Why did it work? It had **one message**. It turned facts into something you could **see**. And it used many modes at once: a sculpture, videos, a website, an app and lessons.

Content that counts doesn't need to be expensive. It needs one clear message, shown in a way people remember.
body.extend:
The **Transport Accident Commission** (TAC) had a familiar problem. Road trauma statistics weren't changing how people thought about their own risk.

In **2016**, it tried a different kind of text. It asked a **trauma surgeon** and a Monash University **crash investigator** how the human body would need to change to survive a crash. Melbourne artist **Patricia Piccinini** then made a life-like sculpture based on their answers: **Graham**.

Graham is confronting on purpose. He has **no neck**, so he can't break it. Each feature responds to a real crash injury.

Graham was first shown at the **State Library of Victoria**, then toured the state. An app let visitors look **beneath his skin**, and schools got lessons to go with him.

The campaign shows multimodal design at work. One message was made visible and memorable, and delivered through sculpture, video, web, app and classroom. Its power came from the idea, not the budget.

model.text:
**Message:** You can cook a real dinner for under $5.

**Audience:** Teens who are about to move out.

**Script (40 seconds)**
- **Hook (0 to 5 s):** “This dinner costs less than a bus fare.”
- **Show (5 to 30 s):** Three quick steps for fried rice. Close-ups of each one. The price pops up beside each item.
- **Proof (30 to 35 s):** The receipt. Total: $4.60.
- **Call to action (35 to 40 s):** “Try it tonight. Send this to a mate who lives on noodles.”

**Test:** I will show three friends and ask what the message was.

teacher.overview: The boss level of Digital Life. Students design and produce a 30 to 60 second video or post with a clear purpose, audience and one message. They write a script for the ear (marking pauses and stress), storyboard shots with attention to framing, salience, sequence and sound, add captions, check facts and permissions, and test the result on their audience. The case study is the TAC's 2016 Meet Graham campaign. Because under-16s can't hold accounts on platforms like TikTok, Instagram and YouTube, publishing happens through class, assembly or school channels.
prep: Check your school's policy on filming students and publishing student work, and on phone use in class.
Arrange devices for filming (phones or school tablets) and a simple free editing app.
Plan where finished videos will be shown: class screening, assembly, school website or newsletter.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** purpose, audience, one message. Hooks: a question, a surprise, a close-up. Check: facts and sources, permission from everyone in it, music rights.

**Storyboard:** 1 hook (close-up and a question); 2 sound (silence for impact); 3 salience (big, centred, high contrast); 4 voice (slow and calm fits the message); 5 sequence (problem, solution, result); 6 call to action (with captions).

**Sort:** “Hi guys, um” — weak; close-up and question — strong; unlicensed song — weak; captions — strong; five tips — weak; fact with source — strong.

**Case study:** our bodies aren't built to survive crashes; a sculpture makes an abstract risk visible and memorable; sculpture, video, website, app, school lessons (and the exhibition tour).

resources.label: eSafety — Social media age restrictions (young people)

realityCheck: **Filming students needs consent.** Check your school's photo and video permissions before anyone films anyone.
**Under-16s shouldn't be told to post publicly.** Plan class screenings or school channels instead.
**Not everyone wants to be on camera.** Offer voice-only, hands-only, animation or slideshow options.
**Editing can eat time.** Keep it to 6 shots and 60 seconds; a phone's built-in editor is enough.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's the natural finale to Digital Life, using what students learned about footprints, influencers and comments to make something of their own.

levels.support: Simpler article and case study, 6 key words, 3-choice quiz, word bank on the annotation, fewer sort cards, a 30-second video with a suggested topic, pair work and sentence starters.
levels.core: Standard version: storyboard anatomy, strong-or-weak choices, the Meet Graham campaign, planning, a scripted video with marked voice, a 6-shot storyboard, and making and testing it with an audience.
levels.extend: Adds call to action and salience to the vocabulary, a quiz question on salience, a script with tone notes, and Level Ups remaking the video to raise an issue and justifying how choices position the audience.
